diagnostic_evidence.quote: In particular, it requires $O(mk^2)$ steps, where $m$ is the number of times we form $B$.

issues.failure_explanation: B is a dense symmetric k x k kernel matrix. Forming it costs O(k^2) kernel evaluations, but computing all its eigenvalues costs O(k^3) (tridiagonalization), as in the cited Golub-Van Loan. The O(k^2) bound holds only after tridiagonalization, so the per-trial cost is O(k^3) and the total is O(mk^3), not O(mk^2).

failure_location.quote: which we may compute in $O(k^2)$ time \cite{golubvanloan}

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace O(k^2) by O(k^3) per trial and O(mk^3) overall, and restate the comparison with n^2 accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised complexity in the introduction and conclusion is misstated. Sub-quadraticity in n for fixed k and m is not affected.
issues.title: Eigenvalues of a dense k x k matrix are not computable in O(k^2); the O(mk^2) cost claim is wrong
issues.why_classification: A local correction of the exponent leaves the method and the qualitative sub-quadratic claim intact.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Since $\nu_i=\mu_i$ for all $i$ and because $T$ has the discrete uniform distribution

issues.failure_explanation: Only the moments r=1..k are assumed equal, and equality for all i does not follow. If it did, the compactly supported discrete uniform laws on S (mass 1/n at n distinct points) and T (mass 1/k at k<n points) would coincide, which is impossible for n>k, so the statement would be vacuous. The later steps need much more than k moments: P_k and its roots depend on mu_0..mu_{2k-1} and D_k on mu_{2k}. These are the steps showing that the b_i are roots of P_k and that the Christoffel weights equal 1/k. With only k moments the Chebyshev-Markov-Stieltjes localisation at k nodes is unsupported, and the claimed k-quantile interlacing is not proved.

failure_location.quote: our assumptions are equivalent to requiring that $\mu_i=\nu_i$ for each $i=1,\ldots,k$, and therefore for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must prove the interlacing from the k matched moments, or require about 2k matched moments and rebuild the construction. The latter forces walks with more than k distinct vertices, which do not exist on K_k, so a coarser quantile resolution with smaller B is also needed.
issues.overall_effect: The theoretical justification that matching k traces of B gives k-quantile sandwich bounds for A's eigenvalues (the interlacing display and the Corollary) is not established. The framework is built on matching exactly k moments.
issues.title: Proof of the moment-matching interlacing proposition silently upgrades k matched moments to all moments
issues.why_classification: The central proof step is invalid, and every repair needs substantially more moment information or a coarser statement, which changes the guarantee and the construction.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: shows, for example, that $b_3\leq a_{10},a_{11},a_{12}\leq b_5$

issues.failure_explanation: With i-th largest ordering, the displayed inequality b_{ceil(jk/n)-1} <= a_j <= b_{ceil(jk/n)+1} is reversed. In the figure (n=15, k=5), b_3 = 9.546 is the third largest and a_10 = 7 is the tenth largest, so b_3 <= a_10 is false. The figure and the conventions b_0=0, b_{k+1}=infinity use ascending order. The Corollary uses descending sigma_j with the opposite inequalities and swapped conventions, yet its proof just says to apply the proposition with S=A and T=B. The reindexing between the two orders (which does work, using k|n) is never carried out.

failure_location.quote: Denote by $a_i$ and $b_j$ the $i$th and $j$th largest elements of $S$ and $T$, respectively

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the proposition with ascending order, or with descending order and reversed inequalities and conventions. Add the short reindexing argument for the corollary.
issues.overall_effect: As written, the proposition is false in its stated ordering, and the corollary's deduction from it is not literally an application.
issues.title: Ordering convention and inequality direction in the proposition are inconsistent with each other, the figure and the corollary
issues.why_classification: A local fix of the ordering convention plus a one-line reindexing preserves all claims.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Then, by our assumption on $\kappa$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:quickdecay},

issues.failure_explanation: The hypothesis says the ratio of integrals equals s+epsilon for all s in [t,1]. At s=1 the ratio is 1, so equality forces epsilon=0, and the hypothesis is not satisfiable for the Gaussian kernels discussed, which only approach s in the limit. If it is read as an additive error bound, the proof only gives the lower bound, since s+epsilon >= (1-epsilon)s is trivial. The upper bound needs s+epsilon <= (1+epsilon)s, i.e. epsilon <= epsilon*s, which is false for s<1. The relative error is epsilon/s, which is huge for s=1/z small (z up to 130.9 in the example). So the two-sided relative bound 1±epsilon is not derived.

failure_location.quote: The second inequality in Equation~\eqref{eq:approxexpect} follows from Equation~\eqref{eq:quickdecay} in a similar way.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the hypothesis as a multiplicative bound |ratio/s - 1| <= epsilon on [t,1], or keep the additive form and conclude 1-epsilon <= ratio <= 1+epsilon/t. Redo the final chain accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The quantitative guarantee (approxexpect) is established only as a lower bound. The upper bound and the meaning of epsilon (in the Gaussian-limit remark and in Section 3) are unsupported.
issues.title: Quick-decay hypothesis as stated forces epsilon=0, and an additive error does not yield the relative upper bound 1+epsilon
issues.why_classification: A contained reformulation of the hypothesis or a weakened conclusion with an epsilon/t factor suffices, and the proof method survives.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: It states that we may always find a distribution with nonnegative support satisfying \eqref{eq:specialdistrib}

issues.failure_explanation: The proof uses the ratio condition with s=1/z_1, i.e. it needs 1/z_1 in [t,1] for Xi-almost every z_1, so supp Xi must lie in [1,1/t]. This is not a hypothesis of the proposition. The only existence result gives nonnegative support, which may include z<1 (then y_j leaves [0,1] and s>1) or very large z (then s<t). In the explicit example, s takes values down to 1/130.9, so t would have to be below about 0.0076. The proposition and the existence result therefore do not combine to give (approxexpect).

failure_location.quote: for some $t\in(0,1)$ and any walk $\pi$ with $|\pi|=l$ on $K_n$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis supp(Xi) contained in [1,1/t] and prove that a distribution satisfying the moment conditions with such bounded support exists, or restate the existence result to give bounded support.
issues.overall_effect: The approximate expected-trace matching is not guaranteed for the distributions the paper actually constructs, and the dependence of t on Xi is hidden.
issues.title: Proof applies the quick-decay condition at s=1/z outside its range [t,1]; the support of Xi is not controlled
issues.why_classification: A missing hypothesis plus a contained new existence or support argument is needed. The overall architecture survives.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: and the third equality follows from the definition of $F$ and the fact that $f_{\psi}=1$ for every $\psi$
applied to uniformly-distributed sets of points in Euclidean space of any dimension

issues.failure_explanation: The points x_i, y_j are scalars drawn from U[0,1], yet kappa acts on R^d and d is claimed to matter. The proof's change of variables scales by 1/z_j, giving y_j ~ U[0,1/z_j] with Jacobian prod z_j and integrals over [0,1]^l. This corresponds to d=1. For y_j = z_j^{-1/d}U[0,1], the interval is [0,z_j^{-1/d}] with density z_j^{1/d}. For genuinely d-dimensional points the integrals are over [0,1]^{dl}, and the quick-decay condition would have to be formulated over cubes of volume s. None of this is carried out, so the case d>1 (the experiments with d=3 and 6, and the intrinsic-dimension application via the role of d) is not covered by the proof.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Redo the setup with x_i in [0,1]^d, y_j uniform on cubes of side z_j^{-1/d}, and a quick-decay condition on [0,s^{1/d}]^{dl}, then repeat the change of variables.
issues.overall_effect: The 'any dimension' claim and the interpretation of d as a tunable dimension parameter are unsupported by the formal result.
issues.title: Proof of the trace-matching proposition only handles d=1 although stated and used for general dimension d
issues.why_classification: The argument structure is the same, but the setup, the hypothesis and the integral computation must be redone consistently for d>1.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: We prove the efficacy of this framework given certain bounds on the kernel function
Because this way of obtaining $Y$ is probabilistic and only guarantees moment matching in expectation
suppose we have $\mathrm{tr}\left(B^r/k\right)=\mathrm{tr}\left(A^r/n\right)$ for $1\leq r\leq k$

issues.failure_explanation: The interlacing corollary requires exact equality of the traces of the actual matrices (equivalently, of the power sums of the actual eigenvalue sets). The proposition gives only an approximate ratio bound on E tr(B^r) versus E tr(A^r). The method then averages the sorted eigenvalues sigma_j(B) over m trials. The power sums of the averaged order statistics are not the expected power sums; by Jensen, (1/k) sum_j (E sigma_j)^r <= E (1/k) sum_j sigma_j^r for r>=2. The gap is the eigenvalue variance, which is large because z (hence the scale of B) varies by orders of magnitude between trials. No concentration or averaging argument is given for B, and the assumption of small variance is made only for A. So the stated efficacy of the framework, and that the averaged eigenvalues bound the quantiles, is only heuristic/empirical.

failure_location.quote: The average $\sigma_j(B)$s should then correspond to bounds for the $k$ quantiles of the eigenvalues of $A$ as in \eqref{eq:interlacing}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must either prove that the averaged sorted eigenvalues of B inherit the interlacing property from expected-trace matching, or restate the claim as a heuristic supported only by numerical evidence.
issues.overall_effect: The main claim that the averaged eigenvalues of B give provable quantile bounds for A is not supported by the formal results, which are expectation-level and approximate.
issues.title: Passage from expected-trace matching to averaged-eigenvalue quantile bounds is unproved, though the paper claims the efficacy is proved
issues.why_classification: The guarantee linking the proved moment statements to the algorithm's output is missing and needs new analysis, or the headline claim must be downgraded.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: If we obtain such distributions which require asymptotically fewer than $O(n^2)$ trials, we would be guaranteed to find bounds for the quantiles of the eigenvalues of $A$ in provably subquadratic time.
Even though $\Xi$ depends on $n$ and $k$, empirically $m$ seems to depends on $k$ alone.

issues.failure_explanation: The total cost is proportional to m, the number of trials. Nothing proves m is independent of n or o(n^2/k^2). The paper's own later remark says that provably sub-quadratic time requires finding better distributions with fewer than O(n^2) trials. The distribution Xi has mean (n-1)/(k-1) and very small probabilities on large scale values, so m may grow with n. The dependence of m on k alone is only empirical, from two (n,k) pairs. The introduction's claim to be the only sub-quadratic method, and the claimed preprocessing independent of the matrix, rest on this unproved assertion.

failure_location.quote: this new framework allows us to find such bounds in subquadratic time relative to $n$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the complexity as conditional on m being o(n^2/k^3), or prove a bound on m for the Xi used. Qualify the claim of being the only sub-quadratic method.
issues.overall_effect: The headline complexity advantage over Nystrom and sketching is unsupported as an unconditional statement.
issues.title: Sub-quadratic time is asserted as established while the paper concedes it is not guaranteed
issues.why_classification: Weakening the claim to a conditional or empirical statement, or adding a bound on m, resolves it without changing the method.
